name: The Auction

CREATORS.summary: Two ad-making regimes ran side by side. The old one was the holding company: WPP, Omnicom, Interpublic and Publicis, each a multi-billion-dollar roll-up of creative shops and media-buying arms, still making the television and print work. Its pay had already changed before the era began — media buying was unbundled from creative in the early 1990s, and by 2003 only about one advertiser in ten still paid its agency a percentage of billings; labour-based fees had won. The new regime had no agency at all. AdWords was self-serve from signup to live ad: the advertiser typed a 25-character headline, two 35-character lines and a display URL into a web form, an automated system approved it, and most ads appeared online immediately. Google's own 10-K sold this as a cost saving — 'because we offer a simple ad format, advertisers can also avoid incurring significant costs associated with creating ads' — and it is the point at which the 15% commission simply stopped existing for a whole class of buyer. Google did build a human layer, but on its own side of the table: field sales and support offices went from 14 countries (2004) to 32 offices in 19 countries (2005) to more than 60 offices in over 20 countries (2008), plus 'AdWords specialists' doing creative maximisation for large accounts. A third creator class appeared: search-marketing agencies and bid-management shops (iProspect, Did-It, Performics, Efficient Frontier) that sold optimisation, not copywriting. The craft skill of the era was not the headline; it was the keyword list.

BUYERS.summary: The era's marginal new buyer was the advertiser who had never bought media before. Overture's model still assumed a screened professional: a 10-cent minimum bid, a $20 minimum monthly spend, and human editorial review of every listing — and it had roughly 80,000 advertisers at the end of 2002 and about 95,000 when Yahoo bought it in mid-2003. AdWords Select removed each of those gates: a 5-cent minimum bid, a one-time $5 activation fee, no monthly minimum, automated approval. That turned the buyer base from a directory of firms into a long tail of plumbers, locksmiths, affiliate marketers and single-product e-commerce sites. Above them sat the same national brands as before, and their internet money was concentrated in exactly the categories that had always lived on measured response: in 2008 retail advertisers were 22% of US internet ad revenue ($5.0bn), financial services 13%, automotive 12%, computing 12%, telecom 9%. The money-type story matters more than the totals. National advertisers still supplied two-thirds of all US ad dollars, and TV brand budgets did not move: broadcast TV spend was $42.1bn in 2002 and $44.5bn in 2007, cable rose from $16.3bn to $26.3bn. What moved was intent money — newspaper classified, directory listings, lead generation, catalogue and mail-order response budgets. eBay, mortgage lead brokers, travel aggregators and comparison shopping sites were the archetypal era-6 heavy spenders, and they bought clicks the way a direct-mail house bought a list.

SELLERS.summary: At the start of the era the paid-search seller was Overture, not Google: Overture booked $667.7m of revenue in 2002 against Google's $439.5m of total revenue, and it owned the distribution deals (MSN, Yahoo, AltaVista, InfoSpace, AOL Europe). Google's answer was not a better auction but a bigger cheque. In May 2002 it took AOL's US search and paid listings from Overture and Inktomi on terms widely reported as an approximately $100m revenue guarantee and an ~85% revenue share — a structure Google's own filings corroborate, since traffic acquisition costs ran at 91% of network advertising revenue in 2002 and 84% in 2003, and AOL alone was 16% of Google's total revenue in 2003. Syndication became the volume engine: network (AdSense) revenue peaked at 48.7% of Google's total in 2004 and was still 41% in Q2 2006. Then the mix inverted as owned search compounded — network fell to 30.8% of revenue by 2008 while Google's total revenue went from $439.5m (2002) to $21,795.6m (2008). Everyone else consolidated or lost: Yahoo bought Inktomi ($235m, Dec 2002) and Overture ($1.6bn+, July 2003) and rebuilt the auction as Panama (Feb 2007); Microsoft launched adCenter and bought aQuantive ($6bn, 2007); Google bought DoubleClick ($3.1bn, 2007). The result was a highly concentrated sell side: the top ten online ad sellers took 72% of US internet ad revenue in Q4 2008, the top 50 took 91%. On the other side of the ledger the classified and directory sellers — newspapers and Yellow Pages publishers — were the losing incumbents.

MEDIUM.summary: The medium mix of 2002-2008 is the strongest evidence against a simple 'digital killed old media' story. Direct mail — measured, keyed, response-priced and a century old — was the single largest US medium for most of the era, rising from $46.1bn (2002) to $60.2bn (2007), well ahead of broadcast television's $44.5bn. Yellow Pages directories, the structural ancestor of paid search, were still growing in dollar terms to about $14.3bn in 2007 (trade sources put the peak at $14.7bn in 2005, a conflict this record keeps open). Cable television grew strongly, broadcast television held, radio was flat, magazines grew, and out-of-home grew — none of them collapsed. Two categories did break: newspaper classified, which fell from $15.9bn (2002) to $10.0bn (2008) with help-wanted classified down 50% inside the era, and newspapers overall, whose print total peaked in 2000 and whose NAA print-plus-online total peaked in 2005 at $49.4bn before falling to $37.8bn in 2008. The internet went from $6.0bn (2002) to $23.4bn (2008) on the IAB/PwC series, with search alone reaching $10.5bn (45% of internet) by 2008. Internet was still only about 7% of total US advertising in 2007. The category boundaries themselves shifted in this window: Coen's own internet line understates the IAB figure by roughly half by 2007, and the Coen/McCann series ends with 2007 data, which is the reason 2008 is a seam year for every long-run chart.

Television taken as one medium (broadcast $44,521m plus cable $26,319m = $70,840m in 2007) remained larger throughout; the direct-mail-is-biggest result depends on Coen booking broadcast and cable separately.

SCALE.summary: US advertising spending grew from $236.9bn (2002) to $279.6bn (2007) on the Coen/McCann series — the last full year that series ever published. Adjusting only for Coen's acknowledged internet undercount lifts 2007 to roughly $290bn. Against GDP the era looks like the opposite of a boom: advertising's share of US GDP peaked in 2000 (2.3% on the McCann series, 2.4% on the IRS corporate-deduction series) and fell through the entire AdWords period, dropping below 2% by 2007. That is the single most inconvenient number for a naive 'Google captured advertising' thesis: the pie did not grow as a share of the economy while search was scaling; money moved between pools. The pools that mattered were direct response and intent. Direct mail, Yellow Pages, newspaper classified and performance-priced internet advertising together made up roughly a third of all US advertising in 2007 (~$99bn of ~$290bn). Search itself was still small in absolute terms — $10.5bn of a ~$290bn market in 2008, about 3.6% — and Google's whole US business was under $11bn. Globally, GroupM put worldwide advertising at $448.6bn for 2007 on a measured-media basis; the same source's US figure of $162.6bn against Coen's $279.6bn is a definitional gap, not a discrepancy, and shows how much of US 'advertising' lives outside measured media.

PRICING.summary: On 20 February 2002 Google replaced CPM AdWords with AdWords Select, and the price of attention changed shape. Ads were ranked by a combination of the advertiser's cost-per-click bid and the ad's click-through rate — expected revenue per impression, not willingness to pay — and the 'AdWords Discounter' charged the winner only enough to hold its position, one cent above the next bid. Google's own 10-K spells out the arithmetic: bids of $1.00, $0.60 and $0.50 produce prices of $0.61, $0.51 and $0.01. From August 2005 a Quality Score set a dynamic minimum bid per keyword, so relevance became a price floor as well as a ranking weight. The entry price was designed to be trivial: a 5-cent minimum bid, a one-off $5 activation fee, no monthly minimum, against Overture's 10-cent minimum bid plus a $20 monthly commitment and human editorial review. The second, larger price in this market was distribution. Traffic acquisition cost — the revenue share paid to syndication and distribution partners — consumed 91% of Google's network advertising revenue in 2002, 84% in 2003 and 79% in 2004, meaning Google's take rate on other people's inventory started at about 9% and reached only about 21% by 2008. On total advertising revenue, TAC peaked at 39% in 2004 and fell to 28.1% in 2008. Elsewhere the old pricing regimes persisted: television still sold on upfront commitments priced from Nielsen ratings, directories on annual per-category contracts, classified by the line, and agencies on labour-based fees rather than the dead 15% commission.

MEASUREMENT.summary: This is the era in which the seller became the auditor. Every price in the search market was set from a count that the seller alone produced: Google recorded the impression, ran the auction, decided which click was valid, and billed against its own log. No third party audited any of it in period — the IAB's Click Measurement Working Group only convened in late 2005 and its guidelines were not published until 2009, and there was no Media Rating Council accreditation of search click counting during the era. The counting crisis arrived as click fraud. Lane's Gifts & Collectibles sued in 2005; Google settled in March 2006 for up to $90 million in advertiser credits, and as part of the settlement the court appointed NYU's Alexander Tuzhilin to examine Google's invalid-click systems — an auditor commissioned by the defendant and paid for by a settlement, which is exactly the institutional novelty. Independent estimators such as Click Forensics put industry-wide click-fraud rates in the mid-teens, figures Google publicly disputed with its own numbers. Google also made the measurement infrastructure free and proprietary: it bought Urchin in April 2005 and relaunched it as Google Analytics in November 2005 at no charge, adding conversion tracking to AdWords, so advertisers measured their results inside the seller's own instrument. Meanwhile the old currency changed too: Nielsen shipped commercial-minute ratings on 31 May 2007, and from the 2007-08 season TV was priced on C3 — average commercial minute plus three days of DVR playback — the biggest change in television's pricing currency since the People Meter.

claims.statement: Independent click-fraud estimators put industry-wide invalid-click rates in the mid-teens during the era — Click Forensics reported roughly 14-17% of ad clicks as fraudulent in 2007-2008 — against Google's own materially lower internal figures, with no accredited third party able to adjudicate.

The two camps are also measuring different denominators - Click Forensics counted invalid clicks in observed traffic, while Google's figure describes clicks surviving its pre-billing filters - so they are not strictly comparable. No accredited measurement body published a competing figure in period. The interval therefore spans both camps as stated (low single digits to the Click Forensics peak) rather than resolving between them; the central sits nearer the third-party estimates because those are the only published industry-wide figures.

TARGETING.summary: The era's targeting unit was the query, not the person. A keyword was a self-declared statement of intent, so matching an advertiser to a searcher required no demographic model at all — which is why the precision of era 6 is best described as intent-level rather than audience-level, and why it competed directly with the two other intent media, classified and directories. AdSense extended the same logic to pages instead of queries: Google bought Applied Semantics in April 2003 and launched AdSense for content on 18 June 2003, reading a page's text and serving keyword ads against it. Around the core, Google widened what could be targeted and what counted as inventory: broad, phrase and exact match; geographic and language targeting; day-parting; smart pricing (2004) discounting network clicks by expected value; site targeting sold on CPM from Q2 2005; and, in April 2004, a policy reversal that let advertisers bid on third parties' trademarks in the US, converting brand names into auctionable inventory and forcing brand owners to bid for their own names. GEICO sued; in December 2004 Judge Brinkema ruled from the bench that selling a trademark as a keyword did not by itself violate the Lanham Act, and the case settled in 2005. Behavioural and audience targeting arrived at the very end of the era, and by acquisition rather than by search: Google-DoubleClick ($3.1bn, April 2007), Yahoo-Right Media ($680m), WPP-24/7 Real Media ($649m) and Microsoft-aQuantive ($6bn) all closed in 2007, setting up era 7's cookie-based machine market.

revenue_per_unit.statement: Google earned roughly 2.2 cents of advertising revenue per search query on its own properties in 2007 ($10.62 billion of Google-owned-site advertising revenue over roughly 480 billion queries), up from roughly 0.47 cents per query in 2002.
revenue_per_unit.unit: USD advertising revenue per Google-owned-site query, 2007
revenue_per_unit.method: Numerator: Google web-sites advertising revenue 2007 = $10,624.705m (Form 10-K FY2008, grade A). Denominator: comScore qSearch measured 37.1bn Google searches worldwide in August 2007, but on a Age-15+, home-and-work basis that excludes public terminals, mobile phones and PDAs - so it is a floor, not a point estimate. Growth-adjusting August back to a calendar-2007 average gives ~34-35bn/month (~410-415bn/yr) on comScore's basis, which sets the interval's UPPER bound for revenue per query ($0.028 at 380bn). The central assumes a modest allowance for comScore's exclusions (~483bn queries, 40bn/month) giving $0.022; the lower bound assumes a 1.5x correction (~664bn queries) giving $0.016. The old interval treated the denominator error as two-sided and its upper bound implied 26.8bn queries/month, below comScore's own August measurement.

sources.name: Google Inc., Form 10-K FY2008, revenue by source
comScore, '61 Billion Searches Conducted Worldwide in August' (Oct 10, 2007; Google 37bn of 61bn)
Kevin Kelly, 'How much does one search cost?' (Oct 11, 2007; 111 billion Google searches per quarter)

cost_to_serve.statement: Serving one Google search query cost roughly 0.35 cents in 2007 — data centres, depreciation, energy, bandwidth and transaction fees, excluding the revenue shared with distribution partners.
cost_to_serve.unit: USD non-TAC cost of revenue per Google query, 2007
cost_to_serve.method: Upper path: Google 2007 cost of revenues $6,649.1m minus traffic acquisition costs $4,933.9m = $1,715.2m of non-TAC cost of revenue (10-K FY2008, grade A). Divided by ~415bn owned-site queries = $0.00413 — an over-estimate, because that cost also carries network ad serving, content acquisition, credit-card fees and amortisation. Lower path: Kevin Kelly (Oct 2007) divided Google's quarterly non-TAC operating cost of $319m by 111bn quarterly searches and got $0.0028. Central set between the two at $0.0035. CI spans a marginal-cost floor (~$0.002, since adding servers is cheaper than the average) to a fully-loaded ceiling (~$0.0055 if a share of R&D is allocated).

sources.name: Google Inc., Form 10-K FY2008, cost of revenues and TAC tables
Kevin Kelly, 'How much does one search cost?' (Oct 11, 2007)

margin.statement: The gross margin on a monetised Google-owned search query was about 85% in 2007 (~2.2 cents of revenue against ~0.35 cents of serving cost, which is where the per-query claims put it — though the margin is not derived that way: the query denominator cancels, so it is computed straight from the FY2008 10-K as 1 - $1,715.2m / $10,624.705m = 83.9%, and the 0.35-against-2.2 pair independently gives 84.1%) — far above Google's reported company-wide gross margin of 59.9%, because the company-wide figure is dragged down by the revenue share paid on syndicated inventory.
margin.method: The query denominator cancels, so compute the margin directly from the FY2008 10-K rather than from the two per-query components: 1 - (non-TAC cost of revenues $1,715.2m / Google-web-sites advertising revenue $10,624.705m) = 83.9%. That is a floor on the owned-search margin, because the $1,715.2m also carries network ad serving, content acquisition, credit-card fees and amortisation that owned-site queries do not cause; stripping those out moves the figure toward the ~88% implied by a Kelly-style narrow non-TAC operating cost. Central set at 85%. Interval spans 78% (generous cost attribution to owned search) to 91% (marginal serving cost only). It deliberately excludes the 64% figure produced by loading a full share of R&D, which is a company-level, not a per-query, cost. Sanity check: Google's reported 2007 gross margin was (16,594.0-6,649.1)/16,594.0 = 59.9% and operating margin 30.6%; the per-owned-query margin is higher because it excludes TAC (30.1% of advertising revenue in 2007), a distribution cost rather than a serving cost.

sources.name: Google Inc., Form 10-K FY2008, consolidated statements of income and TAC tables
comScore, '61 Billion Searches Conducted Worldwide in August' (query denominator)

boundary_notes: Shared with era 5 (1994-2001): AdWords launched in October 2000 as a self-serve CPM product, not an auction; the CPC auction arrives only with AdWords Select on 20 February 2002, which is where era 6 begins. GoTo/Overture, not Google, invented the pay-per-click keyword auction (US Patent 6,269,361) and led paid-search revenue through 2002 ($667.7m vs Google's $439.5m of total revenue); era 5 should carry Overture's 2001 numbers (revenue $288.1m, 1.4bn paid introductions at $0.20 each, ~53,000 advertisers) so the crossover is visible. Era 5 owns the 2001 demand shock: US total ad spend fell from $247,472m (2000) to $231,287m (2001) and US internet ad revenue from $8,087m to $7,134m on the IAB series; era 6 opens with the total at $236,875m and internet at $6,010m in 2002, i.e. internet fell for a second year while the auction was being built. Era 5 also owns the peaks that era 6 inherits as declines: newspaper classified peaked at $19,608.7m in 2000 and help-wanted classified at $8,712.6m in 2000; total US ad spend peaked as a share of GDP in 2000 (2.3% McCann / 2.4% IRS). Shared with era 7 (2008-2026): era 6 closes with US internet ad revenue at $23,448m (IAB/PwC, 2008), search at $10.5bn (45%), performance pricing at 57% of internet revenue, Google total revenue at $21,795.6m with US revenue $10,635.6m, TAC at 28.1% of advertising revenue, Google Network at 30.8% of revenue, and the top ten US online ad sellers holding 72% of revenue. Era 7 owns everything that happens to the mechanism afterwards — header bidding, the 2019 move to unified first-price in Google Ad Manager, RGSP and the squashing/format-pricing knobs exposed in the DOJ trial record, mobile, privacy shocks and the antitrust rulings; era 6 records the auction intact and hands over a signpost, not its death. Data-seam warning shared with the dataset stage: the Coen/McCann series ends with full-year 2007 data, and Coen's own internet line understates IAB/PwC by $10.7bn in 2007, so any splice at 2007/2008 must be annotated rather than joined. Definitional warning shared with era 7: GroupM's measured-media basis puts US 2007 advertising at $162.6bn against Coen's all-media $279.6bn — the difference is direct mail, directories and miscellaneous, the exact categories the era-6 money story turns on.
